# mqlite

> A message queue in a single SQLite file. Peek-Lock delivery, retries, dead-letter
> queues, scheduling, duplicate detection, FIFO groups and topic fan-out — embedded
> in a Go process or served as a tiny HTTP broker. Pure Go, no CGO. MIT licensed.

Public documentation: https://mqlitehq.github.io/.
Relative links below resolve against this website.

NOTE ON VERSIONS: the latest supported release is v0.4.1 (default port 6754,
schema token 7). v0.3.3 is withdrawn, unsupported and retracted by v0.4.0 and later; its
public artifacts remain only for forensic or compatibility inspection and must not
be deployed. This website tracks main, currently source v0.4.1. Runtime access
keys and key-management tools require v0.3.1 or later.
Unified Observe, configured monitor
credentials and the monitoring starter require v0.3.2 or later. Installation commands
below pin v0.4.1. Use the
[v0.4.1 documentation](https://github.com/mqlitehq/mqlite/tree/v0.4.1/docs)
for the supported release's exact API. v0.4.1 is a same-schema patch from v0.4.0.
Schema-5 databases from v0.3.x still require preserving the matching old
binary/database pair and starting v0.4.1 with a fresh database.

- One engine, two front-ends: `mqlite.OpenEmbedded` (in-process, one SQLite file)
  and `mqlite serve` (HTTP broker, default :6754, Bearer-token auth, secure by
  default — a token is auto-generated if none is set).
- Go client choices: `github.com/mqlitehq/mqlite` is the full Go 1.21 module for
  embedded and remote use. MQLite Remote Client for Go keeps the module path
  `github.com/mqlitehq/mqlite-go`; it is the official remote-only,
  standard-library-only companion with a Go 1.13 source floor and omits embedded
  mode, `Observe`, and managed access-key administration.
- Storage: local SQLite (pure-Go driver) or remote Turso/libSQL. A historical
  co-located Turso workload measured about 45 ms p50 for a single durable Send;
  remeasure the current version, database and region before sizing. Both backends
  share successful queue semantics, validation, state transitions and logical errors;
  latency, availability, remote outcome_unknown failures and storage operations
  have different envelopes.
- Wire protocol: JSON over HTTP, one POST per operation, 29 routes in source v0.4.1 under
  /mqlite.v1.QueueService/*, /mqlite.v1.AdminService/* and /mqlite.v1.AuthService/*. Message bodies are
  base64 in JSON. GET / is an open discovery card listing every endpoint.
- Delivery: Peek-Lock (receive → work → settle with a lock_token) or
  receive-and-delete. Exactly one settlement verb per outcome:
  Complete / Abandon / Reject / Defer. Each newly granted claim increments
  delivery_count; Renew extends the same live claim without incrementing it. A 1 s
  reaper returns expired locks to active or to DLQ at the delivery limit. Peek-Lock
  is at-least-once; handlers must be idempotent.
- Lease boundary: new settlements and Renew require the current lock_token and
  locked_until_ms > now; equality is expired, even before the reaper runs. Renew
  before expiry. An unexpired exact-request receipt can replay an already committed
  settlement after its original deadline (same queue, sequence, token, verb and
  effect-changing arguments); it cannot authorize a new effect or revive a lease.
- Receive-and-Delete is explicit at-most-once broker removal: it removes the row
  before returning it and grants no lease:
  empty lock_token and zero locked_until_ms (omitted in JSON), including receive
  attempt replays. The SDK exposes a zero LockedUntil time.
- Retries: the Nth ordinary Peek-Lock claim at max_delivery_count remains a usable
  final attempt and may be renewed or completed. Abandon, lock expiry or startup
  recovery after that failed attempt moves it to the dead-letter state (not a
  separate queue) instead of an ordinary N+1 claim. ReceiveDeferred increments the
  count but currently has no max admission check. Redrive moves dead letters back.
  DLQ age/count/byte settings are asynchronous retention targets, so retained state
  may temporarily exceed them between bounded cleanup passes.
- Ordering: standard (per-group_id FIFO, cross-group parallel), group_fifo
  (group_id required), strict_fifo (whole-queue serial). Order holds across
  crashes and lock expiry. Abandon with delay_ms > 0 parks the message in scheduled
  and keeps blocking its ordered group until due (strict_fifo: the whole queue).
- Pub/sub: topics are implicit; Subscribe(topic, name, filter) creates a backing
  queue per subscription; filters are one expr boolean predicate, fail-closed.
  Queue, subscription and topic names are one disjoint namespace (conflicts 409).
  Retiring the last active subscription makes its implicit topic unavailable for
  fan-out immediately; a deleting mapping reserves the address until cleanup ends.
- Resource deletion (v0.4.0 and later): DeleteQueue and DeleteSubscription require
  manage permission and are empty-only by default. `force=true` is explicit,
  durable authorization to discard every retained state, including locked work.
  Accepted deletion removes the resource from the data plane immediately. A
  `state=deleted` result means cleanup finished in the accepting commit;
  `state=deleting` means bounded cleanup continues and reserves the name. Reconcile
  deleting or unknown outcomes through inventory instead of another delete. The API
  addresses names directly and has no Generation field;
  one owner must serialize deletion with same-name recreation. DeleteQueue rejects
  subscription backing queues. DeleteSubscription requires the exact topic/name pair.
- Subscription lifecycle (v0.4.0 and later): ListSubscriptionsPage provides bounded
  topic filtering, total/count, opaque cursors, lifecycle state and optional deleting
  entries. Subscribe may set a positive `ttl_ms`; omitted or zero creates a permanent
  subscription or preserves an existing lifetime. The broker stores one absolute
  deadline from first creation. Retries, filter updates and message traffic never
  extend it. Expiry removes the subscription from fan-out at the exact deadline and
  preauthorizes forced cleanup. Names remain reserved and count against capacity until
  cleanup completes. Use explicit deletion for normal completion, globally unique
  one-use names for truly temporary subscriptions, and a stable per-instance reply
  subscription plus `correlation_id` for high-rate request/reply traffic. The
  v0.4.1 adds Status and Observe `server_time_ms` for comparing absolute deadlines;
  `sampled_at_ms` may be cached and a browser clock is not authoritative. The bundled
  console groups subscriptions by topic and shows creation, deadline or permanent
  lifetime, and broker-relative remaining lifetime. On current brokers its five-second
  loop calls only Observe; connection, explicit refresh and configuration changes load
  lifecycle inventory, while message operations do not. Older brokers cache the legacy
  fallback instead of repeatedly probing the paged route. This console behavior changes
  neither the schema nor the HTTP/wire API; it uses ListSubscriptionsPage and
  `server_time_ms` present in v0.4.1.
- Maintenance diagnostics (v0.4.0 and later): Observe exposes bounded failure
  details and recovery status. Optional private diagnostic logs retain redacted
  details across restarts; cumulative error counts are not current health.
- Scheduling: deliver at a time (Schedule). Cancel only removes never-delivered
  scheduled messages (delivery_count = 0), not delayed retries. Message TTL starts
  at initial visibility, ends normal delivery and then dead-letters or discards by
  queue policy. A positive queue default is both the default and ceiling; Renew,
  delayed Abandon and scheduler activation never move the fixed deadline. Mixed
  HTTP batches use messages[].ttl_ms; a uniform batch may use the top-level field.
  Duplicate detection is by message_id within a window.
- Transactional outbox (embedded-only): business write + enqueue commit in ONE
  SQLite transaction via mq.Tx.
- Ops: /ui embedded admin console, opt-in authenticated /metrics Prometheus
  (incl. per-RPC latency histograms), /healthz, CLI (26 commands, including the key subcommand group), MCP server (mqlite-mcp, 22 tools in source v0.4.1). The local production
  boundary is one broker per persistent SQLite file; backups and recovery must be
  rehearsed. Use TLS and Bearer authentication for network access.
- Unified observation (v0.3.2 and later): AdminService/Observe, SDK, CLI observe,
  MCP observe, console and Prometheus share one metric contract. Track collection
  success and freshness independently of scrape availability; unavailable values
  are not zero. v0.4.1 adds `server_time_ms`, sampled near response assembly from
  the broker lifecycle clock; queue gauges retain their possibly older
  `sampled_at_ms`. Process counters reset on restart. Use MQLITE_MONITOR_TOKENS for a
  separate read-only collector credential; it permits only Observe and /metrics,
  not payload access, consumption, administration or key issuance. Grafana queries
  Prometheus and does not need the MQLite token. Reuse the supplied dashboard and
  alert rules with an existing collector or the local monitoring starter.
- Prometheus access (v0.3.2 and later): disabled by default (/metrics returns 404 and
  discovery omits metrics). Enable --metrics or MQLITE_METRICS=on to serve on the
  API port; discovery then includes "metrics":"/metrics". Administrator auth must
  stay enabled. Only configured monitor or administrator credentials and managed
  manage keys may scrape. Observe works independently of this switch. Keep the
  collector on a private network; block /metrics at any public API ingress.
  Authentication does not make a public route private. On Fly.io, reuse an
  external collector over the private network instead of adding a monitoring VM.
  v0.4.0 removes the deprecated `mqlite_queue_total` and
  `mqlite_queue_oldest_message_age_ms` aliases. Use
  `mqlite_queue_retained_messages` and `mqlite_queue_oldest_message_age_seconds`;
  divide old millisecond alert thresholds by 1,000. Native Observe JSON keeps
  `queues[].oldest_message_age_ms`.
- Access keys (v0.3.1 and later): configured MQLITE_TOKENS remain full
  administrators. Managed keys are persisted in the same DB and can be created,
  listed, expired and revoked at runtime using SDK/HTTP/CLI/console/MCP.
  send = send/schedule/cancel; listen = receive/settle/renew/peek/queue stats;
  manage includes both and administration/key issuance, including other managers.
  Rights cover the entire broker. Listen is consumption, not read-only auditing.
  Newly generated secrets are mqk_ + 64 lowercase hex; stored as SHA-256 digests,
  never plaintext. Preserve the public 32-lowercase-hex ID before creation.
  Secrets are returned once; a lost response must be reconciled by ID and revoked
  before replacing. Duplicate ID returns key_conflict, never an old secret.
  CLI: key create/list/revoke. MCP: create_key/list_keys/revoke_key.
  List pagination: next_after_id -> after_id; 100 default, 1000 maximum.
  401 unauthenticated or 403 permission_denied is permanent: do not retry forever.
  Revocation affects later requests; already-authorized long polls may finish.
  Environment tokens cannot be listed/revoked through the managed-key API.
- Limits: message body ≤ 1 MiB (configurable), request body ≤ 32 MiB,
  Receive ≤ 256 messages / 20 s long-poll.
- NOT for: log streaming/replay (use Kafka/Redpanda/NATS JetStream), multi-node
  HA clusters (NATS/RabbitMQ), Postgres-native queueing (pgmq/River), or
  sustained six-figure msg/s on one node. Single-writer, single-node by design.

## Docs

- [Concepts](concepts.html): the whole model — queues,
  topics, subscriptions, filters, and the full message lifecycle state machine.
- [Internals](internals.html): schema, concurrency, fencing and recovery.
- [HTTP API reference](api.html): every route, request,
  response, error code and limit.
- [CLI reference](cli.html): the mqlite command-line client —
  broker, produce/consume/administer, embedded or against a broker.
- [Access keys](access-keys.html): permissions, issuance, rotation, expiry and revocation.
- [Operations](operations.html): production scope, backup, restore, upgrade and rollback.
- [Deployment](deployment.html): installation, persistent storage, tokens and TLS.
- [Observability](observability.html): canonical measurements, availability, credentials, dashboard and alerts.
- [Cloud monitoring](observability-cloud.html): private authenticated collection on Fly.io, Alibaba Cloud, Azure and Kubernetes.
- [Turso semantics](https://github.com/mqlitehq/mqlite/blob/main/docs/turso.md): shared business contract, remote failure modes and the one-owner boundary.
- [Retention](https://github.com/mqlitehq/mqlite/blob/main/docs/retention.md): every authorized removal path, cleanup budget and storage-reclamation boundary.
- [Benchmark evidence](https://github.com/mqlitehq/mqlite/blob/main/docs/benchmark.md): reproducible workloads, measured results and limits on what they prove.
- [Conformance contract](https://github.com/mqlitehq/mqlite/blob/main/docs/conformance.md): externally visible invariants and the tests that enforce them.
- [Dependency policy](https://github.com/mqlitehq/mqlite/blob/main/docs/dependencies.md): the Go 1.21 floor, deliberate pins and security checks.
- [For AI agents](agents.html): MCP server setup and a
  copy-paste system prompt for driving the raw HTTP API.
- [Full docs bundle](llms-full.txt): the 14 canonical source documents linked above,
  plus MCP and examples as one plain-markdown file, with source boundaries and
  version metadata preserved. The hand-written agent guide remains a separate page.

## Source

- [GitHub](https://github.com/mqlitehq/mqlite): code, issues, full docs/ tree
  (deployment, Turso, retention, observability, conformance TCK, benchmarks).
- [Concepts source](https://github.com/mqlitehq/mqlite/blob/main/docs/concepts.md).
- [Internals source](https://github.com/mqlitehq/mqlite/blob/main/docs/internals.md).
- [HTTP API source](https://github.com/mqlitehq/mqlite/blob/main/docs/api-reference.md).
- [CLI source](https://github.com/mqlitehq/mqlite/blob/main/docs/cli.md).
- [Operations source](https://github.com/mqlitehq/mqlite/blob/main/docs/operations.md).
- [Deployment source](https://github.com/mqlitehq/mqlite/blob/main/docs/deployment.md).
- [Observability source](https://github.com/mqlitehq/mqlite/blob/main/docs/observability.md).
- [Cloud monitoring source](https://github.com/mqlitehq/mqlite/blob/main/docs/observability-cloud.md).
- [Access key source](https://github.com/mqlitehq/mqlite/blob/main/docs/access-keys.md).
- [MCP source](https://github.com/mqlitehq/mqlite/blob/main/docs/mcp.md).
- [Releases](https://github.com/mqlitehq/mqlite/releases): binaries for
  linux/macos/windows (amd64+arm64), each archive contains mqlite + mqlite-mcp.
- Container image: `ghcr.io/mqlitehq/mqlite:0.4.1` (default port 6754).
  See [Deployment](deployment.html) for persistent storage, authentication and TLS.
- Broker: `go install github.com/mqlitehq/mqlite/cmd/mqlite@v0.4.1`.
- MCP server: `go install github.com/mqlitehq/mqlite/cmd/mqlite-mcp@v0.4.1`.
- Full SDK (embedded + remote): `go get github.com/mqlitehq/mqlite@v0.4.1`
  (Go ≥ 1.21).
- MQLite Remote Client for Go: `go get github.com/mqlitehq/mqlite-go@v0.1.1`
  (Go ≥ 1.13 source compatibility; build production binaries with a supported
  Go release).
